components.name: The 1946 founding
components.explain:
Brennan's began in 1946, when Owen Brennan, an Irish-American New Orleanian, opened the Vieux Carré restaurant on Bourbon Street, across from the Old Absinthe House he already ran. The house legend says a rival teased him that an Irishman's cooking stopped at boiled potatoes, and he set out to prove otherwise with French and Creole cooking.

A lease dispute in 1954 pushed him to plan a move to Royal Street. Owen died in November 1955, before the new house opened; his sister Ella and the family finished the move, and the restaurant opened at 417 Royal Street in 1956.

At the table this is the eighty-year story behind every signature plate: the Hussarde, the turtle soup and the Foster all belong to the family's first decade.

card.front: When and where did Brennan’s first open?
card.back: In 1946, on Bourbon Street, as Owen Brennan’s Vieux Carré restaurant. Owen died in 1955; the family moved the house to 417 Royal Street in 1956.

components.name: The building at 417 Royal Street
components.explain:
The pink house at 417 Royal Street was built in 1795, after the great fire, and soon passed to Don José Faurie. It later became the Banque de la Louisiane, the first bank in Louisiana, and the bank's initials, LB, still sit in the ironwork at the centre of the balcony railing.

From 1841 to 1891 the Morphy family owned it, and Paul Morphy, the chess prodigy many called the unofficial world champion, lived there until his death in 1884.

Brennan's has served here since 1956. Guests often ask how old the building is while they wait for the first course, so point them to the balcony monogram on the way out: it is the easiest way to make the history real.

card.front: What was 417 Royal Street before it was Brennan’s?
card.back: Built in 1795, it became Louisiana’s first bank, the Banque de la Louisiane, whose LB monogram survives in the balcony, then the Morphy family home.

components.name: Breakfast at Brennan’s
components.explain:
Owen Brennan noticed that most New Orleans restaurants served only lunch and dinner. Taking his cue from the popular novel Dinner at Antoine's, he asked why not Breakfast at Brennan's, and built a long, celebratory morning meal: an eye opener, a soup, an egg dish, a flamed dessert.

That idea is still the shape of the day. Breakfast and lunch runs Monday to Friday 9 to 2 and Saturday and Sunday 8 to 2, and the Traditional Breakfast at $80 walks a guest through the whole ritual with its drinks included.

When a guest asks what to order, sell the morning as a sequence, not a single plate: something to start, an egg dish, and the Foster to finish.

card.front: Why is Brennan’s famous for breakfast?
card.back: Owen Brennan built a long, celebratory breakfast when others served only lunch and dinner: eye opener, soup, an egg dish and a flamed dessert.

components.name: The 80th year and the $80 tastings
components.explain:
2026 is Brennan's eightieth year, and the house marks it with two tasting menus at $80 through the year. The Traditional Breakfast includes tasting portions and every listed drink: a Brandy Milk Punch, the Baked Apple, turtle soup or gumbo with a Bloody Bull, Eggs Hussarde with Champagne, the Petite Filet with a red, and Bananas Foster at the table.

The dinner tasting runs from Grand Isle Jewel oysters through the BBQ lobster, Redfish Véronique and the Rohan duck to The Snickers, with a $120 wine pairing.

Read the printed card at lineup: the guide and the live pages disagree on some pours and on the duck course, so quote only what is in your hand that day.

card.front: What does the $80 Traditional Breakfast include?
card.back: Tasting portions of every course and all its listed drinks: milk punch, Baked Apple, soup with a Bloody Bull, Hussarde with Champagne, filet with red, Bananas Foster.

components.name: The closure and the 2014 reopening
components.explain:
Brennan's closed in June 2013 after a foreclosure and a family dispute. Ralph Brennan, a cousin of the former owners, and his partner Terry White bought the building at auction, later acquired the name, and restored the house from top to bottom before reopening in November 2014, with interiors by Richard Keith Langham.

The restoration brought the courtyard and the Chanteclair Room back to life and found ten turtles living in the courtyard, now part of the house's lore.

If a returning guest notices a plate has changed, this is the reason: the menu was refreshed at the reopening and has kept moving since. Keep the answer short and kind: a cousin bought it and brought it back.

card.front: Why did Brennan’s close, and who reopened it?
card.back: It closed in 2013 after a foreclosure and family dispute; Ralph Brennan, a cousin, and partner Terry White bought it and reopened in November 2014.

components.name: The courtyard turtles
components.explain:
During the 2014 restoration the builders found turtles living in the courtyard, and the house adopted them. Ten turtles live there now, named for sauces: five for Escoffier's mother sauces, Béchamel, Velouté, Espagnole, Tomate and Hollandaise, and five for New Orleans sauces, Rémoulade, Ravigote, Bordelaise, Mignonette and Cocktail. Cocktail is the only male.

Each spring the house holds a turtle parade to the fountain, which it calls the slowest second line on earth.

Guests ordering the turtle soup sometimes look nervously at the fountain. Say it before they ask, with a smile: the soup is not the turtles, and the courtyard ten are family.

card.front: Is the turtle soup made from the courtyard turtles?
card.back: No. The ten courtyard turtles, named for five French mother sauces and five New Orleans sauces, are house pets; the soup uses farm-raised turtle.

components.name: Creole and Cajun
components.explain:
Creole cooking is the city's: the food of New Orleans households and restaurants, French in technique, shaped by Spanish, West African, Caribbean, German and Italian cooks, rich in butter, cream and tomato. Cajun cooking is the country food of the Acadians, French settlers who came from Canada to the bayous and prairies west of the city: smoked meats, dark roux and rice.

The two share the trinity, roux and gumbo, and the line between them blurs in every kitchen.

Brennan's is a Creole house that borrows Cajun pantry staples, tasso, andouille and rice dressing. When a guest asks, say Creole is the city, Cajun the country, and our menu is the city with country seasoning.

card.front: What is the difference between Creole and Cajun cooking?
card.back: Creole is the city’s cooking, French technique with butter, cream and tomato; Cajun is the Acadian country cooking of smoked meats, dark roux and rice.

components.name: Escoffier and the mother sauces
components.explain:
Auguste Escoffier, the chef who codified French restaurant cooking in Le Guide Culinaire, organised sauces into families. The mother sauces are espagnole, velouté, béchamel, tomate and hollandaise; every other classical sauce is a daughter, built by adding to one of them.

Brennan's menus read like a lesson in the hollandaise family: plain hollandaise on the Hussarde and Owen, béarnaise on the breakfast hanger, Choron on the Sardou, Foyot on the Chateaubriand. The marchand de vin and bordelaise come from the brown side.

The guide's own advice is that the sauce usually matters more than the protein, for the guest and for the wine. Learn the sauce on each plate first and the rest of the description follows.

card.front: Name the five French mother sauces.
card.back: Espagnole, velouté, béchamel, tomate and hollandaise. Our egg dishes and steaks use the hollandaise family: hollandaise, béarnaise, Choron and Foyot.

components.name: The children’s menus
components.explain:
Brennan's prints a children's breakfast and a children's dinner, each at one set price of $25.00 for guests ten and under. The breakfast price covers fruit, the plate, ice cream and a drink; the dinner price covers salami and cheese, the plate, ice cream and a drink.

The plates are simple on purpose: eggs, French toast, grilled cheese, popcorn shrimp, fried Gulf shrimp, buttered noodles and sautéed Gulf fish, with Brabant potatoes, fries or vegetables.

Tell the parents the whole price at once so there is no surprise, offer the fruit or salami course straight away so the child eats while the adults order, and confirm any cooking style or preference with the kitchen on the ticket.

card.front: What does the $25.00 children’s price include?
card.back: For ten and under: at breakfast fruit, the plate, ice cream and a drink; at dinner salami and cheese, the plate, ice cream and a drink.

components.name: The Roost Bar and Bubbles at Brennan’s
components.explain:
The Roost is the house bar, and birds run through its design: a painted glass mural of birds and birdcages hung over the bar, a nod to Chanticleer, the rooster Owen Brennan chose to stand for early-morning vitality. Bubbles at Brennan's is the afternoon programme there, with sparkling wine, bubbly cocktails and a short list of snacks.

The guide gives the hours as Monday to Friday 2 to 6, with a Champagne sabering on Fridays at 5; an older listing differs, so confirm the days on shift.

The snacks run from Creole spiced nuts at $6 to the Roost Burger at $17. Suggest a snack the moment a drink lands: salt and crunch sell the second glass.

card.front: When is Bubbles at Brennan’s, and what happens on Fridays?
card.back: Per the guide, Monday to Friday 2 to 6 in the Roost Bar and courtyard, with Champagne sabering Fridays at 5; confirm the hours on shift.

components.name: Hollandaise
components.explain:
Hollandaise is a warm emulsion of egg yolks and butter, sharpened with lemon juice or a reduction of vinegar. The yolks are whisked over gentle heat until they thicken, then melted or clarified butter goes in slowly; lecithin in the yolk holds fat and water together in a smooth, pale yellow sauce.

The name means Dutch sauce, though no clear Dutch link has been found. Escoffier counted it among his five mother sauces, and béarnaise, Choron and Foyot are its daughters.

It is fragile: too hot and it scrambles, too cool and it splits. On the Eggs Hussarde and Eggs Owen it is the rich, lemony layer over the egg, the classic half of their two-sauce finish.

card.front: What is hollandaise, and which of our dishes carry it?
card.back: A warm emulsion of egg yolk and butter sharpened with lemon or vinegar reduction; the mother of béarnaise. It tops the Eggs Hussarde and the Eggs Owen.

components.name: Marchand de vin
components.explain:
Marchand de vin means wine merchant. In classical French cooking it is shallots reduced in red wine with a brown stock or demi-glace. New Orleans made its own version: onion and plenty of garlic in place of the shallot, often ham and mushrooms, beef stock and red wine, frequently bound with a roux into a glossy brown sauce. Antoine's made it famous in the city.

The guide's best wording is a savoury red wine and mushroom sauce; calling it a bare reduction undersells it.

On the Eggs Hussarde and Eggs Owen it is the dark, winey half of the two sauces, under the egg. Whether tonight's sauce carries ham or mushroom is a question for the chef before you promise either.

card.front: What is marchand de vin sauce?
card.back: The wine merchant’s sauce: a savoury red wine and mushroom brown sauce, New Orleans style, under the egg on the Hussarde and Owen. Confirm ham with the chef.

components.name: Béarnaise
components.explain:
Béarnaise is hollandaise built on a reduction of white wine vinegar, shallot, tarragon and chervil, finished with fresh tarragon. It is credited to the chef Collinet, who is said to have made it in 1836 for the opening of the Pavillon Henri IV at Saint-Germain-en-Laye, near Paris, and named it for Béarn, the home region of King Henri IV.

The vinegar and tarragon give it a sharper, herbal edge than plain hollandaise, which is why it is the classic sauce for grilled beef.

On the breakfast Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak it is printed as French béarnaise, with a Vital Farms egg alongside. It is also the base for the Choron on the Sardou and the Foyot on the Chateaubriand.

card.front: What makes béarnaise different from hollandaise?
card.back: It is hollandaise built on a vinegar, shallot and tarragon reduction, so it is sharper and herbal; the classic steak sauce, on our breakfast hanger.

components.name: Sauce Choron
components.explain:
Sauce Choron is béarnaise finished with tomato. It is named for Alexandre Étienne Choron, chef de cuisine at the celebrated Voisin restaurant on the rue Saint-Honoré in Paris, who is also remembered for the extraordinary Christmas menu he served during the Siege of Paris.

The tomato is cooked down to a thick paste before it is folded in, so it colours the sauce a soft coral and adds a gentle sweetness without thinning the emulsion.

Brennan's puts Choron on the Eggs Sardou in place of the usual hollandaise. The guide's words for it are tangy and herbal, and that is how to say it to a guest: béarnaise with tomato, brighter than hollandaise.

card.front: What is Choron sauce, and where do we serve it?
card.back: Béarnaise with tomato folded in, tangy and herbal, named for the Paris chef Alexandre Choron. It replaces hollandaise on our Eggs Sardou.

components.name: Sauce Foyot
components.explain:
Sauce Foyot, also called sauce Valois, is béarnaise with meat glaze whisked in. Glace de viande is brown stock reduced until it is thick and syrupy; a spoonful turns pale, sharp béarnaise tawny, deeper and more savoury.

It takes its name from the Restaurant Foyot on the rue de Tournon in Paris, opposite the Senate, named for Nicolas Foyot, who had cooked for King Louis-Philippe. Several dishes there carried the house name.

On the Roasted Chateaubriand it does a necessary job: tenderloin is the leanest, mildest cut on the animal, so a rich, savoury sauce brings the depth the meat lacks. Say it as béarnaise made even richer with a reduced beef glaze.

card.front: What is sauce Foyot?
card.back: Béarnaise enriched with glace de viande, a reduced meat glaze, so it is deeper and more savoury. It goes with our Roasted Chateaubriand.

components.name: Beurre blanc
components.explain:
Beurre blanc, white butter, is a warm sauce of cold butter whisked into a sharp reduction of white wine, vinegar and shallot. There are no egg yolks: the butter alone, added piece by piece over low heat, makes a light, silky emulsion that tastes of cream and acid.

It is a Loire sauce, credited by tradition to Clémence Lefeuvre, who served river fish at an inn east of Nantes; the legend says she made a béarnaise and forgot the yolks and tarragon.

On the Redfish Véronique it is a preserved lemon beurre blanc, salty and perfumed, which suits a flaky fish. Say burr BLAHN, with no K at the end.

card.front: What is a beurre blanc?
card.back: A Loire sauce of cold butter whisked into a wine, vinegar and shallot reduction, no eggs. Ours is preserved lemon beurre blanc on the Redfish Véronique.

components.name: Pecan bordelaise
components.explain:
Bordelaise means two different sauces, and the difference matters. In classical French cooking it is a red wine sauce with shallot, demi-glace and bone marrow, named for Bordeaux. In New Orleans restaurants the word usually means a garlic butter: butter and olive oil with garlic and parsley, spooned over fish or bread.

A pecan bordelaise on a crab-topped Gulf fish with cauliflower purée most likely belongs to the New Orleans family, with toasted pecans worked into the butter.

That is still a reading, not a recipe. The guide's own advice is to confirm with the kitchen which bordelaise it is before you pair wine, because a red wine sauce changes the bottle.

card.front: Which bordelaise is on the Pecan Gulf Fish?
card.back: In New Orleans bordelaise usually means garlic butter, here with pecans; the French one is a red wine sauce. Confirm with the kitchen before pairing wine.

components.name: Mustard cream sauce
components.explain:
A mustard cream sauce is the Burgundian bistro classic behind poulet à la moutarde: shallot softened in butter, a splash of white wine reduced, cream added and simmered, and mustard stirred in at the end. The mustard goes in off the heat, because boiling dulls its bite and can make it bitter.

The result is tangy, rich and pale gold, a sauce that loves crisp poultry.

On the Poussin à la Moutarde it meets something French cooks would not expect: a sweet tea-brined, fried Cornish hen. That pairing, Southern fried chicken under a French bistro sauce, is the whole idea of the dish and the line to give a guest.

card.front: What does à la moutarde mean on our poussin?
card.back: With mustard: a French bistro mustard cream sauce, shallot, wine and cream with mustard stirred in, over our sweet tea-brined fried Cornish hen.

components.name: Creole sauce
components.explain:
Creole sauce is the New Orleans tomato sauce: the holy trinity of onion, celery and bell pepper softened in fat with garlic, then tomatoes, stock, bay, thyme and a measure of cayenne, simmered until thick. It is the backbone of shrimp Creole and of many Creole fish and egg dishes.

It differs from an Italian tomato sauce in its trinity and its pepper, and from a Cajun gravy in its bright tomato.

On the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits it carries tasso, the spiced smoked pork, so the sauce is smoky as well as tangy. That tomato base is what makes our version Creole rather than the bacon and lemon pan gravy of the Carolina dish.

card.front: What is in a Creole sauce?
card.back: A New Orleans tomato sauce built on the holy trinity, onion, celery and bell pepper, with garlic and cayenne; ours carries tasso on the Shrimp & Grits.

components.name: New Orleans barbecue sauce
components.explain:
New Orleans barbecue shrimp is never barbecued. The style was born at Pascal's Manale, Uptown, in 1954, by the family's account, when a regular described a buttery shrimp dish he had eaten in Chicago: head-on shrimp cooked in a pan sauce of butter, black pepper, Worcestershire, garlic and lemon.

The sauce is a pan emulsion, buttery and peppery, not smoky and not tomato. It breaks if it boils or sits.

Brennan's uses the name on two plates, the Louisiana Oysters at breakfast and lunch and the Louisiana BBQ Lobster on the dinner tasting. The house recipe is not published, so describe it as a buttery, peppery New Orleans BBQ sauce and send Worcestershire questions to the kitchen.

card.front: Is New Orleans BBQ sauce smoky or tomato-based?
card.back: Neither: it is a buttery, peppery pan sauce in the barbecue shrimp style from Pascal’s Manale. Send questions on its contents to the kitchen.

components.name: Mignonette
components.explain:
Mignonette is the classic raw bar sauce: finely chopped shallot in vinegar with coarsely cracked black pepper. Mignonnette is the French word for that cracked pepper, which is why the pepper is the ingredient the sauce is named for.

It is spooned onto an oyster by the guest at the table, never poured over in advance, because the acid starts to firm the oyster.

Ours is a preserved Fresno chilli mignonette with parsley on the Grand Isle Jewel oysters: the chilli, salted or pickled and diluted in vinegar, adds a fruity, gentle warmth to the clean, briny oyster. How the chilli is preserved is a good question to ask the chef.

card.front: What is a mignonette, and what is in ours?
card.back: Shallot, vinegar and cracked pepper for raw oysters; ours adds preserved Fresno chilli and parsley, a gentle warmth, on the Grand Isle Jewel oysters.

components.name: Chive rémoulade
components.explain:
Rémoulade is a cold, spiced sauce with two families. The French one is white: mayonnaise with mustard, chopped pickles, capers and herbs, close to tartar sauce. The New Orleans Creole one is pinker and hotter, built on Creole mustard with paprika, cayenne or hot sauce, with or without mayonnaise.

Rémoulade is one of the five New Orleans sauces the courtyard turtles are named for, a sign of how local it feels.

On the Crawfish Meat Pies at the Roost it is a chive rémoulade, cool, tangy and herby against hot pastry. The menu does not print the full recipe, so if a guest asks which style, the kitchen has the answer.

card.front: What is rémoulade, and where is it on our menu?
card.back: A cold spiced sauce, French white or New Orleans pink with Creole mustard; a chive rémoulade comes with the Crawfish Meat Pies at the Roost.

components.name: Crystal gastrique
components.explain:
A gastrique is a French sweet and sour reduction: sugar cooked to caramel, then loosened with vinegar and reduced to a glossy syrup. It balances rich or fried food with acid and sweetness at once.

Crystal is the New Orleans hot sauce made by the family-owned Baumer Foods since 1923, from aged red cayenne peppers, distilled vinegar and salt. It is milder and more vinegary than many hot sauces, so it reads tangy before it reads hot.

On the Roost's Popcorn Shrimp the two meet: a Crystal hot sauce gastrique, sweet, tangy and gently spicy, for dipping crisp fried Louisiana shrimp. Describe it as a sweet and tangy hot sauce glaze.

card.front: What is the Crystal gastrique on the Popcorn Shrimp?
card.back: A sweet and sour reduction made with Crystal, the New Orleans aged cayenne hot sauce since 1923: sweet, tangy, gently spicy with fried shrimp.

components.name: Sweetened condensed anglaise
components.explain:
Crème anglaise is the French pouring custard: milk or cream heated with sugar and vanilla, poured over egg yolks, and stirred gently until it coats the back of a spoon, never boiled or it curdles. It is the base of ice cream and of a Bavarian cream.

A sweetened condensed anglaise is the kitchen's twist: condensed milk, cooked down with sugar, brings a caramel, dulce de leche note to the custard.

On the Pineapple Tarte Tatin it is poured beside the charred pineapple and puff pastry, cool and silky against hot caramel. Say it to a guest as a pouring custard with a caramelised milk flavour.

card.front: What is the anglaise on the Pineapple Tarte Tatin?
card.back: Crème anglaise, a stirred vanilla pouring custard, made with sweetened condensed milk for a caramel note, poured beside the charred pineapple.

components.name: Roux
components.explain:
A roux is flour cooked in fat, stirred constantly, and used to thicken and flavour a sauce or soup. French kitchens cook it white or blond for béchamel and velouté. Louisiana cooks take it much further, to peanut butter, then chocolate or mahogany brown, which gives a toasty, nutty depth; the darker it gets, the more flavour and the less thickening power it has.

A dark roux is the Creole tradition for gumbo and turtle soup, and New Orleans marchand de vin is often roux-bound too. How dark our own kitchen takes each one is a question for the chef.

At the table, a roux is part of why a gumbo or a turtle soup tastes deep rather than brothy. Questions about flour in a dish go to the kitchen.

card.front: What is a roux, and how do Louisiana cooks take it?
card.back: Flour cooked in fat to thicken and flavour. Creole tradition takes it dark for gumbo and turtle soup: toasty depth, less thickening. How dark ours goes, ask the chef.

components.name: The holy trinity
components.explain:
The holy trinity is onion, celery and green bell pepper, chopped and softened together at the start of a Cajun or Creole dish. It is Louisiana's version of the French mirepoix, with bell pepper in place of carrot, which grew more easily in early Louisiana.

The name nods to the Catholic faith of the early settlers, and the phrase was most likely popularised by the chef Paul Prudhomme. Garlic is so often added that some cooks call it the pope.

The trinity is in our gumbo, the turtle soup, the Creole sauce on the Shrimp & Grits and the South Louisiana rice dressing. It is the reason those dishes taste of Louisiana before a single spice goes in.

card.front: What is the holy trinity in Louisiana cooking?
card.back: Onion, celery and green bell pepper softened together: Louisiana’s mirepoix, with bell pepper for carrot. It starts our gumbo, turtle soup and Creole sauce.

components.name: Andouille
components.explain:
Andouille is a coarse-grained, heavily smoked pork sausage, French in origin and remade in Louisiana. German and French butchers along the River Parishes shaped the local style: pork shoulder and fat seasoned with garlic, black and red pepper, stuffed and smoked low over pecan wood and sugar cane for hours. LaPlace calls itself the andouille capital of the world.

It is firm and smoky rather than juicy, made to season a pot rather than to eat alone.

In the Seafood Gumbo it gives the smoky backbone under the shrimp, crab and oysters. Say ahn-DOO-ee, and tell a guest who avoids pork that it is in the gumbo before they order.

card.front: What is andouille, and where is it on our menu?
card.back: A coarse, heavily smoked Louisiana pork sausage with garlic and pepper, smoked over pecan wood. It is the smoky backbone of our Seafood Gumbo.

components.name: Tasso
components.explain:
Tasso is south Louisiana's seasoning meat: strips of pork shoulder cured in salt and sugar, coated thickly in cayenne, garlic and other spices, then hot-smoked until firm. It is sometimes called Cajun ham, but it comes from the shoulder, not the leg, and it is far too spicy and smoky to slice and eat like ham.

Cooks dice it small and cook it into a dish, so a little spreads smoke, salt and heat through the whole pot: jambalaya, red beans, gumbo and cream sauces.

On the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits it seasons the Creole sauce. Both TAH-so and TASS-oh are heard in Louisiana; follow the house habit.

card.front: What is tasso?
card.back: Spiced, cured, hot-smoked pork shoulder used in small amounts as a seasoning meat; called Cajun ham though not leg. It seasons our Shrimp & Grits sauce.

components.name: Louisiana and Gulf shrimp
components.explain:
Louisiana is one of the largest shrimp producers in the country, and the Gulf's brown and white shrimp, caught in the bays and passes of the coast, are the backbone of New Orleans cooking. Brown shrimp come mostly in early summer and taste a little more of iodine and the sea; white shrimp come later in the year and are sweeter and milder.

They are cooked briefly, a couple of minutes at most, or they turn tight and rubbery.

Shrimp appear on our menus in the gumbo, the Shrimp & Grits, the Roost's Popcorn Shrimp and two children's plates. When a guest asks where they come from, the menu's words are Louisiana or Gulf shrimp.

card.front: What do we mean by Louisiana or Gulf shrimp?
card.back: Wild brown and white shrimp from the Gulf coast, the backbone of New Orleans cooking; cooked briefly. In our gumbo, Shrimp & Grits and Popcorn Shrimp.

components.name: Louisiana blue crab and lump crabmeat
components.explain:
Louisiana's crab is the blue crab, caught in the brackish marshes and bays of the coast. Picked crabmeat is sold by grade: jumbo lump is the two large muscles that drive the swimming legs, lump is large body pieces just below it, backfin is smaller flakes, and claw meat is darker and stronger. Cocktail claws are claws with the shell cracked away and the pincer left as a handle.

Lump is sweet, delicate and already cooked, so it is warmed gently, never cooked again.

Our menus use it on the Pecan Gulf Fish, the Crab & Corn Omelette, the en papillote and in the gumbo, with warm claws as a dinner starter. Shellfish questions always go to the kitchen.

card.front: What is lump crabmeat?
card.back: Large pieces of sweet, cooked body meat from the Louisiana blue crab, the grade just below jumbo lump; warmed gently. On the Pecan Gulf Fish and omelette.

components.name: Louisiana oysters
components.explain:
Louisiana oysters are the Eastern oyster of the Gulf coast, grown in the warm, brackish water where the Mississippi meets the sea. Most are wild from public and leased reefs; a growing number are farmed in cages off the bottom. They are larger, milder and less salty than many northern oysters, which is why New Orleans cooks them as often as it eats them raw.

Cooked oysters want only seconds: they are done when the edges curl, and a moment longer shrinks them.

On our menus oysters come cooked in New Orleans BBQ sauce at breakfast and lunch, in the gumbo, and as the smoky dressing on the Creole Caesar. How many come per order is a lineup question.

card.front: How do Louisiana oysters differ from northern oysters?
card.back: Gulf oysters from brackish Mississippi water: larger, milder and less salty, so New Orleans cooks them as often as it eats them raw. Edges curl when done.

components.name: Gulf fish of the day
components.explain:
When the menu says Gulf fish, it means the day's catch from the Gulf waters along the coast rather than a fixed species. Kitchens in New Orleans buy what the boats bring: drum, sheepshead, snapper, grouper, triggerfish, speckled trout and others, each with its own texture, from flaky and delicate to firm and meaty.

The preparation is built to suit a range of fish, so the sauce and garnish stay the same while the fillet changes.

That makes one habit essential: know today's fish and how it is cooked before service. It is on the Pecan Gulf Fish, the Gulf Fish en Papillote and the children's sautéed Gulf fish, and every guest will ask what it is tonight.

card.front: What should you know before selling a Gulf fish dish?
card.back: Gulf fish means the day’s catch, not one species: drum, snapper, trout and others. Learn tonight’s fish and preparation at lineup before you sell it.

components.name: Redfish
components.explain:
Redfish, or red drum, is a Gulf fish with a black spot near the tail and firm, mild, slightly sweet white flesh that holds together in the pan. It became a national craze around 1980 when the chef Paul Prudhomme blackened it at K-Paul's in New Orleans, and demand grew so fast that Louisiana banned commercial redfish fishing later that decade to protect the stock.

So restaurant redfish today is usually farm-raised or comes from other sources; where ours comes from is a question for the chef.

On the Redfish Véronique it stands in for the sole of the French classic: firm enough for a beurre blanc and pickled grapes, mild enough to let them speak.

card.front: What is redfish, and why is its source a question?
card.back: Red drum, a firm, mild Gulf fish. The blackening craze of the 1980s led Louisiana to ban commercial catch, so ask the chef where ours comes from.

components.name: Creole tomatoes
components.explain:
Creole tomatoes are Louisiana's summer tomatoes. The name began with growers in St. Bernard and Plaquemines parishes, below New Orleans, who let their tomatoes ripen on the vine in rich river soil and sold them as Creole; the LSU AgCenter later also bred a variety called Creole. Today the word is used for tomatoes grown in Louisiana.

They are prized for being picked ripe: juicy, sweet and sharp, with a soft skin, so they do not travel far.

On the Creole Tomato Tostada they are served raw with heirloom tomatoes, burrata and smoked tomato water. The dish follows the season, so expect it to change when the tomatoes finish.

card.front: What is a Creole tomato?
card.back: A vine-ripened Louisiana tomato, first from St. Bernard and Plaquemines river soil: juicy, sweet and sharp. Served raw on our seasonal Creole Tomato Tostada.

components.name: Okra
components.explain:
Okra is the green seed pod of a plant in the mallow family, brought to the Americas from West and Central Africa. Sliced and simmered, it releases a silky thickness that thickens soups; fried or dried crisp, it loses that texture and turns nutty. The word gumbo itself most likely comes from a West African word for okra, ki ngombo.

Southern and Creole cooks fry it, pickle it and stew it with tomatoes.

On our menus it is crisp: a housemade okra tostada under the Creole tomatoes, and fried okra chips on the Shrimp & Grits. The menu does not list okra in the gumbo, so do not promise it there.

card.front: Where does okra come from, and how do we serve it?
card.back: A seed pod from West and Central Africa that gave gumbo its name. We serve it crisp: the okra tostada and the fried okra chips on the Shrimp & Grits.

components.name: Louisiana popcorn rice
components.explain:
Popcorn rice is a Louisiana aromatic long-grain rice that really does smell of popcorn as it cooks. The aroma comes from a compound called 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline, the same molecule that perfumes basmati and jasmine rice and fresh popcorn, and Louisiana aromatic rice carries it in large amounts.

It cooks up firmer and more separate than jasmine, which is what a gumbo wants: grains that hold their shape in the broth.

Our Seafood Gumbo is served over popcorn rice. If a guest notices the nutty, toasty smell, that is the rice, not the roux, and it is a nice detail to share when the bowl lands.

card.front: What is popcorn rice, and why does it smell like popcorn?
card.back: A Louisiana aromatic long grain carrying 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline, the popcorn and basmati aroma molecule. Firm, separate grains under our Seafood Gumbo.

components.name: Grits
components.explain:
Grits are dried corn ground coarse and simmered slowly in water or milk until creamy, the Southern answer to polenta. Stone-ground grits keep more of the corn's germ and flavour and take longer to cook than quick grits; hominy grits are made from corn treated with alkali.

They are a blank, comforting base that takes on butter, cheese and sauce.

We serve them two ways: Cheddar Grits as a breakfast side, and a fried pimento cheese grit cake, crisp outside and creamy inside, under the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits. Whether ours are stone-ground, and whose corn, are good questions for the kitchen.

card.front: What are grits?
card.back: Coarse-ground dried corn simmered slowly until creamy, the Southern polenta. We serve Cheddar Grits as a side and a fried pimento cheese grit cake.

components.name: Pimento cheese
components.explain:
Pimento cheese is the South's best-loved spread: grated sharp cheddar bound with mayonnaise and chopped sweet red pimientos. It began in New York around the 1870s as soft Neufchâtel mixed with imported Spanish peppers, then moved south, where cooks remade it with cheddar and mayonnaise and claimed it as their own.

It is tangy, creamy and a little sweet, and it melts beautifully.

On the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits it is folded into the grits before they set, then the cake is fried, so the outside is crisp and the inside creamy and cheesy. That fried grit cake is what most surprises guests who expect a bowl.

card.front: What is pimento cheese, and how is it used on our Shrimp & Grits?
card.back: Cheddar, mayonnaise and sweet pimientos, a Southern spread born in New York. It is folded into our grits, which are set and fried into a crisp cake.

components.name: Housemade Creole spice
components.explain:
Creole seasoning is a dry blend built on paprika, cayenne and black pepper, with garlic and onion powder, dried thyme and oregano, and salt. It gives warmth, colour and savour more than raw heat, and every kitchen keeps its own proportions.

Brennan's makes its own, and the menu names it on the dinner Creole Hanger Steak; the breakfast hanger, the potato on the Eggs Owen and the Roost's spiced nuts are seasoned in the same style.

What is in the house blend is not printed, so if a guest asks about a particular spice, or how hot it is, the kitchen has the answer. In general, describe it as warm and savoury rather than fiery.

card.front: What is in Creole seasoning?
card.back: A dry blend of paprika, cayenne and black pepper with garlic, onion, thyme and oregano: warm rather than fiery. Ours is housemade; the kitchen has the recipe.

components.name: Blackening
components.explain:
Blackening is a young Louisiana technique. The chef Paul Prudhomme created it at K-Paul's around 1980: a fillet dipped in melted butter, coated in a paprika-led spice blend, and laid in a dry cast-iron skillet heated past smoking. The spices toast to a dark, almost black crust in seconds while the inside stays moist.

Prudhomme used it because his small kitchen had no grill, and the hot pan imitated char. Blackened redfish became a national craze.

Our Blackened Tofu uses the method on local tofu. The butter in the classic method is why the guide asks you to check with the kitchen before calling the dish vegan.

card.front: What is blackening, and who made it famous?
card.back: A spice-coated food seared in a smoking-hot dry cast-iron pan to a dark crust; Paul Prudhomme’s technique from around 1980. Used on our Blackened Tofu.

components.name: Frying, golden and crisp
components.explain:
Deep frying cooks food submerged in hot oil, usually around 175 to 190 C. A coating, flour, cornmeal, batter or crumb, dries and browns into a crust while the inside steams in its own moisture. Oil that is too cool makes food greasy; too hot burns the outside before the inside cooks. Fried food is drained on a rack and served at once.

Fried food sells itself at a bar, and our menus use it widely: popcorn shrimp, fried Gulf shrimp, fried pickles, fries, the fried grit cake and okra chips, crispy artichokes and the fried Cornish hen.

Questions about coatings, shared fryers or what oil is used go to the kitchen every time.

card.front: What makes fried food crisp rather than greasy?
card.back: Oil at the right heat, about 175 to 190 C, browns the coating fast while the inside steams; drained on a rack and served at once. Fryer questions go to the kitchen.

items: Fried Gulf Shrimp with French Fries

components.name: Brown butter
components.explain:
Brown butter, beurre noisette in French, is butter cooked past melting until its milk solids toast to the colour of hazelnuts and it smells nutty and sweet. It must be stopped at that moment, often with lemon or vinegar, because a few seconds more and it burns bitter.

That nutty depth is why it appears across our menus in different forms.

On the Louisiana Crab Claws it becomes a warm brown butter vinaigrette, sharpened with acid; the spinach in the Turtle Soup is wilted in brown butter; and the financiers in the Blackberry Trifle are made with it, which is what makes them taste buttery rather than cakey.

card.front: What is brown butter, and where do we use it?
card.back: Butter cooked until its milk solids toast nutty, beurre noisette, stopped with acid: the crab claws’ vinaigrette, the turtle soup’s spinach, the trifle’s financiers.

components.name: The poached egg
components.explain:
A poached egg is cooked out of its shell in water held just below a simmer, often with a splash of vinegar to help the white set. The fresher the egg, the tighter the white. After about three minutes the white is set and the yolk still runs; restaurant kitchens often poach ahead, hold the eggs in iced water and reheat them for a few seconds at service.

The runny yolk becomes part of the sauce when the guest cuts in.

Our poached eggs sit at the heart of the Eggs Hussarde and the Eggs Sardou. They come soft unless the guest asks otherwise, and the guide says to check with the kitchen before promising firmer eggs.

card.front: How are the eggs on the Hussarde and Sardou cooked?
card.back: Soft poached: cooked out of the shell in water below a simmer until the white sets and the yolk runs. Check with the kitchen before promising firmer.

components.name: Eggs cooked to order
components.explain:
Eggs any style covers the short list a breakfast cook makes every day. Sunny side up is fried on one side only, white set and yolk liquid; over easy is flipped briefly; over medium and over hard cook the yolk further. Scrambled eggs are stirred as they set, soft or firm; a soft-boiled egg is simmered in its shell for about six minutes so the yolk stays runny.

The server's job is to ask and to write it exactly on the ticket.

Our menus print a soft-boiled egg on the Eggs Owen and a sunny-side-up egg on the Duck Confit Waffle and the breakfast hanger, and offer an Egg Any Style side and the children's eggs. Confirm the styles the kitchen offers at lineup.

card.front: What are the common egg styles to ask a guest?
card.back: Sunny side up, over easy, over medium, over hard, scrambled soft or firm, poached, soft-boiled. Write the style exactly on the ticket.

items: Eggs Any Style with Toast and Bacon

components.name: Leidenheimer bread
components.explain:
Leidenheimer is the bakery behind New Orleans French bread and the po-boy. George Leidenheimer, from Deidesheim in Germany, started it in 1896, moved it to Simon Bolivar Avenue in 1904, and soon switched from dense German loaves to the light, airy loaf with a thin, crackly crust that the city preferred.

That loaf shatters when you bite it and stays tender inside; it is the standard for po-boys across the city.

On the Creole Caesar it becomes Leidenheimer crisps, thin toasted slices that replace croutons. Telling a guest the crisps are made from the city's po-boy bread turns a garnish into a piece of New Orleans.

card.front: What is Leidenheimer, and where is it on our menu?
card.back: The New Orleans bakery since 1896 whose light, crackly French loaf is the po-boy standard. Toasted into the crisps on our Creole Caesar.

components.name: Pecans
components.explain:
The pecan is a hickory native to the Mississippi valley and the South, the nut New Orleans cooks reach for first. It is rich, buttery and sweet, softer than an almond, and it toasts quickly, so it is roasted gently.

Louisiana cooks used pecans in place of the almonds of French recipes, which is how the praline became a pecan candy and how pecan butters came to dress fish.

Pecans appear across our menus: in the crumble on the Baked Apple, on the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake, in the pecan bordelaise on the Pecan Gulf Fish and in the pralines on the bread pudding. Nut questions always go to the kitchen and the service note.

card.front: Why are pecans everywhere on a New Orleans menu?
card.back: The native Southern nut, rich and buttery; Louisiana cooks used it in place of French almonds. On our Baked Apple, coffee cake, Gulf fish and pralines.

components.name: Crème fraîche
components.explain:
Crème fraîche is cream thickened and soured gently by lactic cultures, the French cousin of sour cream. It is richer and milder than sour cream, with a fresh, slightly nutty tang, and it does not split when warmed.

A spoonful brings cool, tangy richness against something warm, sweet or rich.

We use it three ways: sweetened beside the Baked Apple on the breakfast tasting, whipped on the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake, and as the cool, silky layer in the Steak Tartare Cannoli. Say krem FRESH, and describe it to a guest as a slightly tangy cultured cream.

card.front: What is crème fraîche, and where do we use it?
card.back: A cultured French cream, richer and milder than sour cream with a gentle tang: sweetened on the Baked Apple, whipped on the coffee cake, in the tartare cannoli.

components.name: Collard greens
components.explain:
Collard greens are broad, sturdy leaves of the cabbage family, a pillar of Southern cooking. Traditionally they are simmered for a long time with smoked pork until silky, and the cooking liquid, the pot likker, is prized in its own right.

Cooked quickly or pickled, they keep a pleasant chew and a cabbagey bite.

Our menus use them two ways. On the Louisiana Oysters they are pickled, a sharp bite that cuts the rich BBQ sauce the way a mignonette would. On the Pecan Gulf Fish they are wilted, earthy greens beside the cauliflower purée. Neither is the long-simmered pot of a Sunday table, which is worth saying if a guest expects it.

card.front: How do we serve collard greens?
card.back: Pickled on the Louisiana Oysters for a sharp bite against the rich sauce, and wilted on the Pecan Gulf Fish, not the long-simmered Southern pot.

components.name: Baked apple with oat and pecan crumble
components.explain:
The Baked Apple starts with a whole apple, peeled, cored and trimmed flat so it stands. A crumble of rolled oats, pecans, raisins, brown sugar and cinnamon is packed on top, and the apple bakes until a skewer slides through with no resistance. The brown sugar melts into the apple's juices and caramelises, which is where the glaze comes from.

It is the French baked apple meeting the British crumble, warm and soft under a little crunch.

It is the first plated course of the Traditional Breakfast, after the Brandy Milk Punch. Which apple the kitchen uses, and whether the tasting portion is whole or half, are good lineup questions.

card.front: How is the Baked Apple on the breakfast tasting made?
card.back: A whole apple, peeled and cored, baked soft under an oat, pecan, raisin, brown sugar and cinnamon crumble that caramelises into a glaze; served with sweetened crème fraîche.

components.name: Filet mignon
components.explain:
Filet mignon is a small steak cut from the narrow end of the beef tenderloin, the muscle along the spine that does almost no work. That makes it the most tender cut on the animal and also one of the mildest, so it relies on its sauce and garnish for savour.

A petite filet is a small portion that cooks quickly: seared hard, finished gently and rested for a few minutes so the juices settle.

On the Traditional Breakfast it is the fourth course, with a crisp potato rösti, garlic spinach and a 4 oz pour of Côtes du Rhône. Take the guest's temperature when you take the tasting order, not when the course fires.

card.front: When do you take the temperature for the tasting’s Petite Filet?
card.back: With the tasting order, at the start. Filet mignon is the tender, mild narrow end of the tenderloin; ours comes with rösti, garlic spinach and Côtes du Rhône.

components.name: Potato rösti
components.explain:
Rösti is the Swiss potato cake from the Bern region: potato grated, pressed into a hot pan with butter or fat, and cooked slowly on both sides into a thick, golden disc that is crisp outside and soft within. Raw grated potato gives the most crunch; restaurants often par-boil the potatoes, chill them and grate them the next day so the cake holds together.

The Bernese say it with a soft sh, which is why the guide's RUHSH-tee is right.

Under the Petite Filet Mignon on the breakfast tasting it does the job of the classic steak potato: crisp texture and starch to catch the meat's juices.

card.front: What is a rösti?
card.back: A Swiss grated potato cake from Bern, pressed in a hot buttered pan until crisp outside and soft within. It sits under our Petite Filet Mignon.

components.name: Garlic spinach
components.explain:
Garlic spinach is fresh spinach wilted quickly in a hot pan with oil or butter and sliced garlic, then squeezed of its water and seasoned at the last moment so it stays bright green rather than grey.

It is the simplest of the greens on our menus, light where the creamed spinach is rich.

On the Petite Filet Mignon it brings the savour that a mild filet lacks: garlic, iron and a little bitterness to balance the beef and the crisp rösti. If a guest asks how it differs from the Sardou's spinach, the answer is that this one is wilted with garlic, not creamed with Parmesan.

card.front: How does the filet’s garlic spinach differ from our creamed spinach?
card.back: It is wilted quickly with garlic, light and green; the creamed spinach on the Sardou and as a side is bound with cream and Parmesan.

components.name: Lobster
components.explain:
Lobster on a New Orleans menu comes from the cold waters of the North Atlantic; the Gulf has spiny lobsters but no clawed lobster. The meat is sweet, firm and rich, and it toughens quickly if it boils, so kitchens usually blanch and shell it first, then finish it gently in a sauce.

New Orleans cooks have long dressed it in local styles, and here it wears the city's barbecue shrimp sauce.

On the dinner tasting's Louisiana BBQ Lobster it sits on a white bean stew with 'nduja. The guide asks you to confirm the night's BBQ sauce at lineup, because the house's version has changed over the years.

card.front: Where does the lobster on the BBQ Lobster come from?
card.back: Clawed lobster comes from the cold North Atlantic, not the Gulf. Ours is finished gently in New Orleans BBQ sauce over a white bean and ’nduja stew.

components.name: ’Nduja
components.explain:
'Nduja is a soft, spicy pork sausage from Calabria, at the toe of Italy, made around the village of Spilinga. Pork trimmings and fatback are ground with a large share of sun-dried Calabrian chilli, stuffed, lightly smoked and cured. At room temperature it is soft enough to spread like a pâté.

Warmed, it melts into whatever it touches, carrying fat, salt and a slow red-pepper heat.

In the white bean stew under the Louisiana BBQ Lobster it plays the part andouille plays in red beans: a little pork melting into the beans, so every spoonful is rich and gently hot. Say en-DOO-yah, and warn guests who are shy of spice.

card.front: What is ’nduja?
card.back: A spreadable, chilli-hot pork sausage from Spilinga in Calabria. It melts into the white bean stew under our BBQ Lobster, giving a slow red-pepper heat.

components.name: White bean stew
components.explain:
A white bean stew is dried white beans soaked and simmered slowly with aromatics and stock until they are creamy but still whole, the idea behind a French cassoulet or a pot of Louisiana beans. The beans drink up fat and flavour, so they make a soft bed for something rich.

Kept loose and spoonable, the stew catches the sauce from whatever sits on top.

Under the Louisiana BBQ Lobster it carries 'nduja, so the beans are creamy, porky and gently hot, and the buttery BBQ sauce runs into them. Whether the 'nduja is cooked into the beans or added as a finishing spoonful is a good question for the chef.

card.front: What sits under the Louisiana BBQ Lobster?
card.back: A creamy white bean stew with ’nduja, like a spicy Calabrian cousin of Louisiana beans; it catches the buttery BBQ sauce from the lobster.

components.name: Rohan duck
components.explain:
Rohan is not a breed but a proprietary cross created for D'Artagnan, a specialty meat company. It brings together the heritage Mallard and the Pekin, and the birds are raised for D'Artagnan on a farm in New York State's Catskills, without antibiotics, to about eleven weeks, longer than most commercial ducks.

The name honours the Rohan family of Brittany. The meat is rosy, tender and milder than wild duck, with a good layer of fat under the skin.

We use it twice: the roasted breast on the dinner tasting and the confit leg on the Duck Confit Waffle. Say a special cross raised in New York, and do not call it a breed.

card.front: What is a Rohan duck?
card.back: A proprietary Mallard and Pekin cross raised for D’Artagnan in New York’s Catskills: rosy, tender, mild meat. Our tasting breast and confit waffle leg.

components.name: Roasting a duck breast
components.explain:
A duck breast carries a thick layer of fat under the skin, and the cook's job is to render most of it away while keeping the meat rosy. The skin is scored in a tight crosshatch, the breast goes skin-down into a cold or moderate pan, and the fat melts out slowly as the skin crisps. A short turn on the flesh side, a finish in the oven and a rest of a few minutes follow, then it is sliced across the grain.

Duck breast is served pink, like a steak; cooked through it turns grey and livery.

On the dinner tasting the Rohan breast comes with cane syrup-glazed peaches and candied hazelnuts. The usual doneness is medium-rare to medium; confirm at lineup.

card.front: How is duck breast usually served, and why?
card.back: Pink, medium-rare to medium, after the fat is rendered from scored skin; cooked through it turns grey and livery. Confirm the kitchen’s temperature at lineup.

components.name: Louisiana cane syrup
components.explain:
Cane syrup is sugar cane juice boiled down in open kettles until thick, with nothing taken out. Molasses is what remains after sugar has been crystallised and removed, so cane syrup is sweeter, lighter and milder, with a buttery caramel taste rather than molasses's bitter edge. Steen's of Abbeville has made it since 1910, after a freeze threatened a cane crop.

It is a Louisiana pantry staple poured on biscuits, baked into cakes and used to glaze meat.

On the Roasted Rohan Duck Breast it glazes peaches, sweet and caramelised against rich duck. The menu does not name a brand, so say Louisiana cane syrup, a lighter cousin of molasses.

card.front: How does cane syrup differ from molasses?
card.back: Cane syrup is cane juice simply boiled down with nothing removed, so it is sweeter and lighter; molasses is what is left after sugar is taken out.

components.name: Candied hazelnuts
components.explain:
Candied hazelnuts are toasted hazelnuts coated in caramelised sugar, the same family as a French praline. Hazelnuts are sweet, buttery and slightly bitter in the skin, and toasting brings out their aroma.

The coating must stay dry and glassy; humid air turns it sticky within an hour, so they are made close to service.

On the Roasted Rohan Duck Breast they give crunch and a toasty sweetness against the soft duck and glazed peaches. The guide notes that the autumn version of the duck course may change to a hazelnut-crusted plate, so read the printed tasting card at lineup before describing it.

card.front: What gives crunch on the Roasted Rohan Duck Breast?
card.back: Candied hazelnuts, toasted nuts in a glassy caramel coating, a praline cousin; toasty and sweet against the duck and cane syrup peaches.

components.name: The English trifle
components.explain:
A trifle is an English layered pudding with centuries of history: sponge or biscuits soaked in sherry or juice, fruit, custard and whipped cream, built in a glass bowl so the layers show. It was a dish for gatherings and a way to use up cake.

Our Blackberry Trifle rebuilds it in French pastry terms. Fruit curds take the place of custard, small financiers replace the sponge, and a coconut chia pudding is the modern layer.

It is built in a glass so the guest sees the colours. Served as a starter on the breakfast and lunch menu, it suits the middle of the table while the eggs are cooking: tart rather than sugary.

card.front: What is a trifle, and how does ours differ?
card.back: An English layered pudding of sponge, fruit, custard and cream. Ours uses blackberry and lemon curds, coconut chia pudding and blackberry financiers.

components.name: Blackberry and lemon curds
components.explain:
A fruit curd is a cooked spread of fruit juice, sugar, egg yolks and butter, stirred over gentle heat until it thickens to coat a spoon, then chilled until set. Lemon curd is the British classic; blackberry curd uses the purée of the fruit, which gives a deep purple colour and a tart, jammy taste.

Curds are richer and sharper than jam and silkier than custard.

In the Blackberry Trifle the two curds are the bright, tart layers, purple and yellow, that keep the dessert from tasting sugary. They are made ahead and set cold, so the trifle can be built quickly to order. The service note lists what the curds contain.

card.front: What is a fruit curd?
card.back: Fruit juice, sugar, egg yolks and butter cooked until thick and set cold: tart, rich and silky. Blackberry and lemon curds are the bright layers of our trifle.

components.name: Coconut chia pudding
components.explain:
Chia seeds come from a plant of the mint family native to Central America. Soaked in liquid for several hours, each seed swells and wraps itself in a soft gel, so a spoonful of seeds sets a whole bowl of milk into a pudding without cooking.

Made with coconut milk it is lightly sweet and tropical, with a texture like tapioca.

In the Blackberry Trifle it is the creamy, modern layer between the tart curds. The guide suggests mentioning the seedy texture before a guest orders, since some people love it and some do not; coconut is listed on the service note.

card.front: What is the chia pudding layer in the trifle?
card.back: Chia seeds soaked in coconut milk until they swell into a gel and set the milk: creamy, lightly sweet, tapioca-like. Mention the seedy texture.

components.name: Financiers
components.explain:
A financier is a small French cake of ground almonds, egg whites, sugar, a little flour and brown butter, baked in a small mould. The standard account credits a Paris pâtissier named Lasne, whose shop stood near the stock exchange around 1890; he shaped them like little gold bars for the traders, and the name stuck.

The brown butter is what makes them taste rich and nutty, with crisp edges and a moist centre.

In the Blackberry Trifle they are blackberry financier biscuits, the trifle's answer to sponge. The guide notes they are traditionally made with almond flour and asks you to confirm with the kitchen.

card.front: Why is a financier shaped like a gold bar?
card.back: A Paris pâtissier near the stock exchange shaped these almond and brown butter cakes like gold bars for traders around 1890. Ours sit in the trifle.

components.name: French toast, pain perdu
components.explain:
French toast is pain perdu, lost bread: stale bread rescued by soaking it in egg and milk, often with sugar and vanilla, and frying it in butter. In New Orleans it is an old Creole breakfast. The bread must be thick and slightly dry, or it soaks to mush; the pan must be moderate, so the custard centre sets before the outside burns.

Brioche makes the richest version, soft and custardy inside with a caramelised crust.

Our Framboise French Toast uses housemade citrus brioche, sold as a starter to share, and the children's breakfast offers a vanilla French toast with berries and whipped cream.

card.front: What does pain perdu mean, and where is it on our menu?
card.back: Lost bread: stale bread soaked in egg and milk and fried in butter. Our Framboise French Toast uses citrus brioche; children get vanilla French toast.

items: Vanilla French Toast with Fresh Berries and Whipped Cream

components.name: Housemade citrus brioche
components.explain:
Brioche is a French bread enriched with eggs, butter and a little sugar, so it bakes up golden, soft and almost cake-like, with a fine, tender crumb. The dough is slow and sticky to make, and the butter is worked in after the dough has built its stretch.

A citrus brioche adds orange or lemon zest for perfume.

The kitchen bakes its own for the Framboise French Toast, sliced thick so it can soak up custard without falling apart. That housemade detail is worth saying: it is why the French toast is rich and custardy inside rather than bready.

card.front: What kind of bread is in the Framboise French Toast?
card.back: Housemade citrus brioche, an egg and butter enriched French bread with zest, sliced thick so it soaks up custard and stays rich inside.

components.name: Mascarpone mousse
components.explain:
Mascarpone is a fresh cheese from Lombardy, made by setting cream with acid and draining it. It is rich, mild and spoonable, closer to clotted cream than to a cream cheese, and it is the cheese in tiramisu.

Whipped with a little sugar and cream, it becomes a light mousse that holds its shape on warm food.

On the Framboise French Toast the mascarpone mousse is the cool, creamy layer against the warm brioche and the sharp raspberries. The guide's description, a whipped Italian cream cheese, is a fair word for guests. Say mahs-kar-POH-neh, four syllables.

card.front: What is mascarpone?
card.back: A rich, mild fresh cheese from Lombardy made from cream, the cheese in tiramisu. Whipped into a mousse on our Framboise French Toast.

components.name: Raspberry coulis and framboise
components.explain:
Framboise is French for raspberry, which is where the French Toast gets its name. A coulis is a smooth fruit sauce: berries cooked briefly or simply puréed with sugar and a little lemon, then pushed through a fine sieve so no seeds remain.

Raspberries are among the sharpest of the soft fruits, so the coulis cuts richness.

On the Framboise French Toast the raspberry comes twice, as a bright red coulis and as fresh local raspberries, against the brioche and the mascarpone mousse. Say frahm-BWAHZ for the name and koo-LEE for the sauce.

card.front: What do framboise and coulis mean?
card.back: Framboise is French for raspberry; a coulis is a smooth, sieved fruit sauce. Our French toast gets a raspberry coulis and fresh local raspberries.

components.name: Café brûlot
components.explain:
Café brûlot is New Orleans' flaming after-dinner coffee. Antoine's credits Jules Alciatore, the founder's son, with café brûlot diabolique in the late nineteenth century: brandy and orange liqueur flamed in a bowl with cinnamon, clove and a long spiral of orange and lemon peel, then ladled into strong coffee at the table. Brûlot comes from brûler, to burn.

It is one of the city's great tableside rituals.

Brennan's borrows its flavours for the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake: chicory coffee and bittersweet chocolate cake, pecans, a spiced citrus glaze and whipped crème fraîche. The drink itself is not on our list, so sell the cake as the coffee's flavours, not the flame.

card.front: What is café brûlot, and how does our coffee cake use it?
card.back: New Orleans’ flaming spiced coffee with brandy and citrus peel, from Antoine’s. Our coffee cake borrows its flavours: chicory coffee, chocolate, spiced citrus glaze.

components.name: Chicory coffee
components.explain:
Chicory is a plant whose root is roasted and ground and mixed with coffee. The French stretched coffee with it during the blockades of the Napoleonic wars, and New Orleans, a French city and a great coffee port, kept the habit, most famously when the Union blockade cut off coffee during the Civil War.

It stayed because people liked it: chicory adds a roasty, slightly bitter, chocolatey depth and a smooth body.

Our New Orleans style coffee is made with chicory, and the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake bakes chicory coffee into a bittersweet chocolate cake, where it deepens the chocolate. Questions about caffeine go to the service note.

card.front: Why does New Orleans coffee contain chicory?
card.back: Roasted chicory root stretched coffee in French blockades and the Civil War, and New Orleans kept it for its roasty, chocolatey depth. It is in our coffee cake.

components.name: Fried saltine crumble
components.explain:
Saltines are thin, crisp, lightly salted crackers, the cracker that sits on every Gulf Coast oyster bar beside the hot sauce and horseradish. Crushed, fried in butter or oil and seasoned, they become a crunchy crumble.

It is the raw bar's oyster cracker turned into a garnish.

On the Louisiana Oysters the fried saltine crumble gives crunch against the soft oysters and the rich BBQ sauce, and it is added at the last moment so it stays crisp. The guide lists saltines on the service note; questions go there and to the kitchen.

card.front: What is the crunchy topping on the Louisiana Oysters?
card.back: A fried saltine crumble: the Gulf oyster bar’s cracker, crushed and fried, added at the last moment for crunch against the oysters and BBQ sauce.

components.name: Burrata
components.explain:
Burrata is a fresh cheese from Puglia in southern Italy: a pouch of mozzarella filled with stracciatella, shreds of curd soaked in cream. Cut open, the centre spills out soft and milky.

It is best at room temperature and torn rather than sliced; cold burrata is firm and loses its sweetness.

On the Creole Tomato Tostada it is the creamy partner to the raw Louisiana tomatoes, the way mozzarella partners tomato in a caprese. The guide's line, mozzarella with a creamy centre, is exactly right for a guest. Say boo-RAH-tah.

card.front: What is burrata?
card.back: A Puglian mozzarella pouch filled with cream-soaked curd, soft and milky inside, served at room temperature. The creamy partner on our Creole Tomato Tostada.

components.name: Okra tostada and smoked tomato water
components.explain:
A tostada is a flat, crisp fried tortilla of the Mexican kitchen, used as a base for toppings. Ours is housemade with okra; the menu does not say whether it is made on masa or wheat, which matters for some guests, so ask the kitchen.

Tomato water is the clear juice that drips from salted, puréed tomatoes hung in cloth overnight: pale gold, intensely tomatoey and light. Smoking it adds a gentle campfire note.

On the Creole Tomato Tostada the tomato water goes on last, so the tostada stays crisp for the first bites. Tell the guest to eat it soon after it lands: the crunch fades within minutes.

card.front: What is smoked tomato water?
card.back: The clear juice of salted, puréed tomatoes strained overnight, then smoked: intensely tomatoey and light. Poured on last so our okra tostada stays crisp.

components.name: Fines herbes
components.explain:
Fines herbes is the classical French mix of four soft herbs: parsley, chives, tarragon and chervil, chopped finely and used fresh. Chervil tastes of mild anise and parsley, tarragon of stronger anise, chives of gentle onion.

They are added at the very end of cooking, because heat blackens tarragon and chervil and kills their perfume.

On the Louisiana Crab Claws they are tossed through the warm brown butter vinaigrette at the last moment, a fresh green lift against nutty butter and sweet crab. If a guest asks what the green flecks are, name the four herbs.

card.front: What are fines herbes?
card.back: The classic French four: parsley, chives, tarragon and chervil, added fresh at the end. They finish the brown butter vinaigrette on our Louisiana Crab Claws.

components.name: Warm crab claws
components.explain:
Cocktail crab claws are blue crab claws with the shell cracked away from the meat and the pincer left on as a handle. They arrive already cooked and chilled, so the kitchen only warms them through; cooking them again tightens the meat onto the cartilage and makes it hard to pull.

Guests eat them with their fingers: hold the pincer, bite the meat and slide the cartilage out.

Our Louisiana Crab Claws are served warm in the brown butter vinaigrette, which surprises guests who expect cold claws, so say served warm aloud and bring napkins and a plate for the shells. Whether they can be served chilled on request is a question for the chef.

card.front: How do guests eat the Louisiana Crab Claws?
card.back: With fingers: hold the pincer, bite the meat, slide the cartilage out. Say they are served warm, and bring napkins and a plate for shells.

components.name: Grand Isle Jewel oysters
components.explain:
Grand Isle is the barrier island at the edge of the Louisiana coast. Grand Isle Jewels is a brand launched in April 2025 by JEDCO, the Jefferson Parish economic development commission, with the island's off-bottom oyster farmers.

Off-bottom farming raises oysters in cages that float or hang above the seafloor. The cages are tumbled and sorted, which shapes a deep, clean cup and a tidy shell, and the method is gentler on a storm-damaged coast than dredging wild reefs.

We serve them raw with a preserved Fresno chilli mignonette, at dinner and as the first course of the dinner tasting. Know the count per order, and ask the chef whether to tell the farming story.

card.front: What are Grand Isle Jewel oysters?
card.back: Louisiana oysters farmed in cages above the seafloor off Grand Isle, a 2025 brand from JEDCO and the island’s farmers: deep, clean cups. Served raw.

components.name: Raw on the half shell
components.explain:
Oysters on the half shell are shucked to order: the knife goes in at the hinge, the top shell comes off, and the adductor muscle is cut cleanly so the oyster sits loose in its cup with its liquor. They are bedded on crushed ice and reach the table cold.

The liquor, the salty juice in the shell, is part of the taste; a good shucker never pours it away.

The Grand Isle Jewel oysters are served this way. The guide flags a raw shellfish advisory on this dish: read the service note, and send every question about raw seafood to the kitchen or the manager rather than answering it yourself.

card.front: What should a server know when selling raw oysters?
card.back: They are shucked to order and served cold with their liquor. Read the raw shellfish advisory on the service note and send questions to the kitchen.

sources: research/dossier-the-kitchen.md (Grand Isle Jewel Oysters, cook’s notes)

components.name: Fresno chilli
components.explain:
The Fresno chilli was released in 1952 by Clarence Brown Hamlin and named for Fresno, California. It looks like a jalapeño and sits in the same heat band, roughly 2,500 to 10,000 Scoville units, but it has thinner walls, ripens quickly to bright red and tastes fruitier. A fully red Fresno can be a little hotter than a green one.

Preserved, salted or pickled, it softens and spreads its warmth evenly through a liquid.

In the mignonette on the Grand Isle Jewel oysters it is diluted in vinegar, so it reads as a gentle, fruity warmth rather than real heat, which is why the guide calls it mild.

card.front: How hot is the Fresno chilli in our mignonette?
card.back: A jalapeño-level chilli from 1952, fruitier and thinner-walled; preserved and diluted in vinegar it reads as a gentle warmth on the Grand Isle oysters.

components.name: Steak tartare
components.explain:
Steak tartare is raw beef, trimmed of every sinew and chopped finely by hand, then seasoned at the last moment. The Paris brasserie version mixes in shallot, capers, cornichons, mustard and a raw yolk, served with toast or fries.

Hand-cutting matters: ground beef turns pasty and grey, while a knife keeps a clean, silky texture.

In the Steak Tartare Cannoli the seasoned beef is piped into a crisp potato shell with crème fraîche and finished with grated cured egg yolk, two bites held in the hand. The guide carries a raw beef advisory on this dish; read the service note and send questions to the kitchen.

card.front: What is steak tartare?
card.back: Raw beef trimmed and finely hand-chopped, seasoned at the last moment. Ours is piped into a crisp potato cannoli; read the raw beef advisory on the service note.

components.name: The potato cannoli shell
components.explain:
A cannoli is a Sicilian pastry: a fried tube of dough filled with sweet ricotta. The Steak Tartare Cannoli borrows the shape and makes the shell from potato instead, a thin potato sheet wrapped around a mould and fried until it holds a crisp tube.

The shells are fried ahead and kept dry and warm; an hour in humid air and they soften.

Piped end to end with tartare and crème fraîche, the shell gives a crunch that replaces the toast or fries of a brasserie tartare. How the shell is made, and whether it shares a fryer, are questions for the kitchen, as the guide asks.

card.front: What is the cannoli shell on the Steak Tartare Cannoli made of?
card.back: Potato: a thin sheet fried crisp around a mould in the shape of a Sicilian cannoli, replacing the toast or fries of a brasserie tartare.

components.name: Egg yolk bottarga
components.explain:
Bottarga is salted, pressed and dried fish roe, grey mullet in Sardinia and tuna in Sicily, grated over pasta like a savoury cheese. Egg yolk bottarga borrows the idea: yolks are buried in salt and sugar for a day or more, rinsed and dried at low heat until firm enough to grate.

The result is rich, salty and deeply savoury, a golden snow on the plate.

On the Steak Tartare Cannoli it is grated over the top in place of the raw yolk of a classic tartare. It is the only dish on the current menus with it, so do not describe cured yolk as a standing house preparation.

card.front: What is egg yolk bottarga?
card.back: Egg yolks cured in salt and sugar, dried firm and grated like bottarga, the cured fish roe: rich and salty, over our Steak Tartare Cannoli.

components.name: Creole turtle soup
components.explain:
Turtle soup came to New Orleans in the French colonial era and became a Creole classic. Where the turtle soups of London and Philadelphia were clear consommés, Creole cooks made a dark, thick soup: turtle meat with a brown roux, the trinity, tomato, stock and Worcestershire, finished with sherry, lemon and chopped hard-boiled egg.

Many turtle soups, in restaurants and in cans, are stretched with veal or beef, and mock turtle has none at all. That is why our menu prints 100% turtle meat.

It is a Brennan's signature at both meals and the second course of the Traditional Breakfast. Say the word turtle plainly; many guests are trying it for the first time.

card.front: Why does our menu say 100% turtle meat?
card.back: Many turtle soups are stretched with veal or beef, and mock turtle has none. Ours is all turtle: a dark, roux-thickened Creole soup finished with sherry.

components.name: Turtle meat
components.explain:
Restaurant turtle in Louisiana is farm-raised freshwater turtle, usually snapping turtle, bought from licensed suppliers; it is not a wild or endangered species. The meat is dark, firm and rich, somewhere between veal and dark chicken, with plenty of gelatin, which gives the soup its body and its silky coat on the palate.

It is chopped finely and simmered for a long time, so it is tender and spread through the soup rather than served in chunks.

When a guest hesitates, describe the taste rather than the animal: rich, meaty and savoury, like a deep beef stew. The current supplier is a question for the chef, not a guess.

card.front: Where does the turtle in our soup come from?
card.back: Farm-raised freshwater turtle, usually snapping turtle, from licensed suppliers; never the courtyard turtles. Ask the chef for the current supplier.

components.name: Aged sherry
components.explain:
Sherry is the fortified wine of Jerez in southern Spain, aged in a solera of barrels where young wine is blended into older wine over years. The dry, aged styles, amontillado and oloroso, taste of walnuts, toffee and salted caramel, with a sharp, dry finish.

A spoonful of sherry stirred into a rich soup at the end lifts it, the way lemon lifts fish: the acidity and nutty aroma cut through fat and gelatin.

Aged sherry finishes our Turtle Soup, along with brown butter spinach and grated egg. Whether it is added in the kitchen, at the pass or at the table is a lineup question, and guests who avoid alcohol should be told it is there.

card.front: Why is sherry added to the turtle soup?
card.back: A dry, aged sherry, nutty and sharp, lifts the rich soup at the end the way lemon lifts fish. Tell guests who avoid alcohol it is there.

components.name: Brown butter spinach and grated egg
components.explain:
Our Turtle Soup is finished with two garnishes that go back to the old Creole recipes. Spinach is wilted in brown butter, so it is nutty and soft, and folded through the soup. Hard-boiled egg is grated finely over the top.

The egg adds richness and a soft texture; the body of the soup comes from the roux and the gelatin of the turtle and stock, not from the egg, whatever older notes say.

Together with the aged sherry they make the bright, nutty finish the guide describes. If a guest asks what the yellow and green flecks are, name them: grated egg and brown butter spinach.

card.front: What are the green and yellow flecks in the turtle soup?
card.back: Brown butter spinach, wilted and nutty, and finely grated hard-boiled egg, which adds richness; the body comes from the roux and the turtle’s gelatin.

sources: research/dossier-the-kitchen.md (Turtle Soup, one slip in the guide)

components.name: Gumbo
components.explain:
Gumbo is the dish that tells Louisiana's history in one bowl. Its name most likely comes from a West African word for okra; its roux comes from French cooking, made darker in Louisiana; its filé, ground sassafras leaves, came from the Choctaw; and Spanish, German and Caribbean cooks all added to it.

There are countless gumbos: seafood, chicken and andouille, and the green gumbo z'herbes. A seafood gumbo uses a dark roux and a stock made from the seafood shells, with the seafood added at the end.

Ours is Shrimp, crab, oysters and andouille over popcorn rice, a signature at both meals and the alternative to turtle soup on the Traditional Breakfast.

card.front: What cultures came together in gumbo?
card.back: West African okra and its name, French roux, Choctaw filé, plus Spanish, German and Caribbean cooks. Ours is seafood with andouille over popcorn rice.

components.name: The Caesar salad
components.explain:
The Caesar salad was created in 1924 at Caesar Cardini's restaurant in Tijuana, just over the border, a draw for visitors escaping Prohibition. The story is that it was improvised at the table: romaine, a raw egg yolk, olive oil, Parmesan, Worcestershire, lime and toasted bread. Cardini relied on the anchovy in the Worcestershire rather than adding whole anchovies; those came later.

It became the most copied salad in the world, often made tableside.

Our Creole Caesar gives it a Gulf accent: gem lettuce, a smoked oyster dressing in the briny role of anchovy, Grana Padano and Leidenheimer crisps in place of croutons.

card.front: Where did the Caesar salad come from?
card.back: Caesar Cardini’s restaurant in Tijuana, 1924, improvised at the table. Our Creole Caesar swaps anchovy for a smoked oyster dressing and croutons for Leidenheimer crisps.

components.name: Gem lettuce
components.explain:
Little Gem is a small, sweet lettuce, a cross between romaine and butterhead: crisp, upright hearts with tender, slightly buttery leaves. It holds a thick dressing without wilting and is often served halved or quartered through the core so each wedge stays together.

It is milder and sweeter than a full romaine and keeps its crunch longer on the plate.

On the Creole Caesar it carries the smoked oyster dressing, the Grana Padano and the Leidenheimer crisps. If a guest asks why it is not romaine, the answer is that gem is the sweeter, crisper little cousin.

card.front: What lettuce is in the Creole Caesar?
card.back: Little Gem, a small, sweet cross of romaine and butterhead with crisp hearts that hold a thick dressing without wilting.

components.name: Smoked oyster dressing
components.explain:
A Caesar dressing is an emulsion of egg yolk, garlic, lemon, Worcestershire, oil and cheese. Ours blends smoked oysters into it, so the oysters take the briny, savoury role that anchovy usually plays, and add a gentle smoke.

It is the change that makes the salad a Gulf dish: the oyster is the most New Orleans of ingredients.

Because the dressing is made with oysters, the guide asks servers to treat the Creole Caesar as a shellfish dish: flag it on the ticket and check with the kitchen for any guest who asks about shellfish. Whether the dressing also carries anchovy is a question for the chef.

card.front: What makes the Creole Caesar dressing different?
card.back: Smoked oysters are blended into the Caesar emulsion in place of anchovy, briny and smoky. Flag it as shellfish on the ticket and check with the kitchen.

components.name: Grana Padano
components.explain:
Grana Padano is a hard cheese from the Po Valley of northern Italy, made from partly skimmed cow's milk and aged for at least nine months, usually longer. It has protected status, and its origin story credits Cistercian monks in the Middle Ages. Grana means grainy, for its crumbly, crystalline texture.

It is milder, younger and sweeter than Parmigiano Reggiano, and it melts smoothly.

We use it twice: shaved over the Creole Caesar and finishing the Shells & Cheese. A guest who asks whether it is Parmesan can be told it is its milder Po Valley cousin.
